historical_timeline.summary: Palpitations and pain about the heart at Plymouth before the Beagle sailed.
Palpitations; rest in the country on his doctors' advice.
First mention of periodical vomiting in a letter.
Incessant vomiting described in a letter, after a winter of weekly vomiting.
Began about three months of the water cure at Great Malvern (other accounts give March 12).
Began his health diary, kept until January 1855.
A short talk at the Linnean Society brought on 24 hours of vomiting.
Died in Downe, Kent, aged 73, after anginal attacks and heart failure in his last years.

claims.statement: Charles Darwin was born on February 12, 1809, in Shrewsbury, Shropshire, England.
Darwin died on April 19, 1882, in Downe, Kent, aged 73.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Record the death as a fact without detail.

claims.statement: While waiting at Plymouth to sail on the Beagle in late 1831, Darwin was troubled with palpitations and pain about the heart, and consulted no doctor for fear of being judged unfit for the voyage.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Past history only; the earliest recorded palpitations.

claims.statement: In September 1837 he had palpitations and, on his doctors' advice, went to the country to recover.
Darwin first mentioned periodical vomiting in a letter to W. D. Fox in June 1840.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Past history; the documented start of the episodic vomiting.

claims.statement: In February 1849 he described incessant vomiting to Richard Owen, and in March 1849 he wrote that he had been bad all winter, with dreadful vomiting every week, that his hands trembled, and that his head was often swimming.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the synthetic presenting episodes at the index visit.

claims.statement: In March 1849 Darwin took his family to Dr. James Manby Gully's water-cure establishment at Great Malvern for about three months; the treatment included heating by spirit lamp, cold towel rubs, cold foot-baths, a wet compress on the stomach, simple food, and short walks.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Fixes the index age near the start of the water cure; the treatment itself is not modeled.

claims.statement: Darwin kept a health diary from July 1, 1849, to January 16, 1855, which records near-daily flatulence and notes the acidity of his vomit.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documents the interepisode symptoms; claim only, after the index date.

claims.statement: Over his adult life he had gastrointestinal distress, including vomiting, retching, and bowel irregularity, with headaches, fatigue, trembling, faintness, dizziness, and skin problems including eczema.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented symptom complex the episode draws on.

claims.statement: In April 1861 he wrote that a short talk at the Linnean Society brought on 24 hours of vomiting.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documents social stress as a trigger; claim only, after the index date.

claims.statement: A British Medical Journal note on his medical history, published after his death, said that in his last years the heart and great vessels were degenerating, anginal attacks became more frequent, signs of heart failure appeared, and he died in one of these attacks.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documents the final illness; claim only, after the episode.

claims.statement: Cyclic vomiting syndrome, perhaps from a mitochondrial DNA disorder, has been proposed as the cause of his illness.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation. The synthetic episode's provisional modern diagnosis does not confirm it.

claims.statement: Chagas disease, contracted during the Beagle voyage, has been proposed as the cause of his illness.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation; not tested or coded in the episode.

claims.statement: Systemic lactose intolerance has been proposed as the cause of his illness.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation; not tested or coded in the episode.

claims.statement: Panic disorder with agoraphobia has been proposed as the explanation of his illness and secluded life.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective psychiatric interpretation; not coded. The episode screens for anxiety without diagnosing an anxiety disorder.

claims.statement: Other proposed explanations include hyperventilation, neurasthenia, hypoglycemia, other allergies, Crohn's disease, Helicobacter pylori infection, systemic lupus, Meniere's disease, and psychological or psychosomatic causes.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretations; none is used in the episode.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Evaluation and first six months of care of recurrent stereotyped vomiting episodes in a 40-year-old man: a symptom diary, the Rome IV criteria for cyclic vomiting syndrome and its red flags, a cannabis and substance history (to exclude cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome), a work-up between episodes to exclude other causes (blood count, metabolic and liver panels, lipase, urinalysis, TSH, morning cortisol, celiac serology, CT enterography, and upper endoscopy), a baseline ECG, and anxiety and mood screens (GAD-7, PHQ-9). Management follows the 1842 ANMS and Cyclic Vomiting Syndrome Association guideline: amitriptyline prophylaxis titrated to about 1 mg/kg with ECG checks of the QTc, an abortive plan of nasal sumatriptan and ondansetron at the prodrome, an individualized emergency department protocol, trigger management, and relaxation training. The diagnosis stays provisional because it is clinical, and none of the historical theories of his illness is treated as confirmed.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Darwin is a 40-year-old man evaluated six weeks ago for more than a year of episodes of nausea and repeated vomiting, who returns for his results and is seen by gastroenterology on the same day. His diary records three episodes since the first visit, each starting in the early morning or after a social evening, with half an hour to an hour of nausea, sweating, trembling hands, a racing heart, and a swimming head, then vomiting many times over 18 to 30 hours. He lay in a dark room and sipped water, and did not need emergency care. Between episodes he has wind and tires by the afternoon but does not vomit. His weight is steady. He confirmed again that he has never used cannabis and does not take long hot baths or showers during episodes. The blood and urine tests and ECG at the first visit were normal, the CT enterography two weeks later was normal, and the upper endoscopy two weeks ago was normal, with normal duodenal biopsies.

ros.finding: Episodic vomiting; wind between episodes; no blood in vomit or stool; no nocturnal pain
Tired after episodes; weight steady
Racing heart only in the prodrome; no chest pain or fainting
No migraine headaches, weakness, or visual loss; swimming head only in the prodrome
Worry about episodes in company; no low mood most days; no thoughts of self-harm

exam.finding: Well between episodes; weight 71.4 kg
Regular rhythm at 76 per minute; blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, with no drop on standing
Soft, non-tender, no distension or succussion splash
Cranial nerves and gait normal

assessment_plan.assessment: Gastroenterology confirms that he meets the Rome IV criteria: stereotyped episodes of acute vomiting lasting less than a week, many more than three in the past year and two in the past six months, at least a week apart, without vomiting between them. The work-up excludes obstruction, mucosal disease, pancreatitis, thyroid and adrenal disease, celiac disease, and metabolic causes, and he does not use cannabis. The diagnosis is clinical and recorded as provisional. With episodes every one to three weeks that stop his work, the disease is moderate to severe, and prophylaxis is advised
plan: Start amitriptyline 25 mg at bedtime and raise it by 25 mg every two weeks by portal message to 75 mg (about 1 mg/kg), as gastroenterology advises
Abortive plan: sumatriptan 20 mg nasal spray and ondansetron 8 mg dissolving tablet together at the first sign of the prodrome
Emergency department letter with his diagnosis and an agreed treatment protocol, to carry with him
Trigger plan: regular small meals, regular sleep, and planning around travel and social events
Relaxation breathing taught today; cognitive behavioral therapy offered, and he will consider it
ECG when the dose reaches 50 mg and again at 75 mg

referral.question: Recurrent stereotyped episodes of nausea and vomiting for more than a year in a 40-year-old man, about every one to three weeks and almost weekly this winter. Please advise whether this is cyclic vomiting syndrome, whether the work-up is complete, and on prophylaxis, abortive treatment, and an emergency plan
referral.urgency: Routine, within six weeks, on the same day as his results visit
referral.pertinent_history: More than a year of episodes, each beginning with half an hour to an hour of nausea, sweating, trembling hands, a racing heart, and a swimming head, followed by repeated vomiting for 12 to 36 hours; he lies still in a dark room until it passes. Between episodes he has troublesome wind and tires easily but does not vomit. Episodes cluster around social gatherings, speaking to groups, overnight travel, short sleep, and long gaps without food. He has never used cannabis and has no habit of hot baths or showers during episodes. One or two glasses of wine a week; does not smoke. No weight loss, blood in vomit or stool, nocturnal pain, migraine headaches, or neurological symptoms. Past history of palpitations in his twenties. Blood count, electrolytes, creatinine, glucose, calcium, albumin, liver tests, lipase 32 U/L, TSH 1.6, morning cortisol 14.2, tissue transglutaminase IgA 1.2 with total IgA 210, and a urine dipstick all normal, drawn between episodes. ECG: sinus rhythm, QTc 412 ms. GAD-7 8 and PHQ-9 6, with no thoughts of self-harm. CT enterography and upper endoscopy ordered. Blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, pulse 78, weight 71.6 kg, BMI 21.4. No medicines
questions: Do his episodes meet the Rome IV criteria for cyclic vomiting syndrome, and is anything in the history against it?
Is the work-up complete, or are further tests needed (for example a gastric emptying study or brain imaging)?
Do you advise prophylaxis, and if so which medicine, at what dose, and with what monitoring?
What abortive treatment should he take at the prodrome?
What should an emergency department do when an episode does not settle?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Darwin, a 40-year-old writer and naturalist, is seen at the request of Dr. Ashworth for more than a year of stereotyped vomiting episodes. His diary shows three episodes in the six weeks since his first visit, each 18 to 30 hours, after a prodrome of nausea, sweating, trembling, palpitations, and a swimming head lasting half an hour to an hour. Vomiting is frequent at the peak, then he sleeps. Between episodes he does not vomit, though he has wind and tires by the afternoon. Episodes follow social evenings, travel, short nights, and missed meals. He has no headaches with or between episodes, no dizziness on standing, and no weight loss, nocturnal pain, or blood. He has never used cannabis, by any route, and does not bathe compulsively. He drinks little alcohol and takes no medicines. He worries about being taken ill in company and has begun to avoid gatherings

assessment.assessment: He meets the Rome IV criteria: stereotyped episodes of acute-onset vomiting lasting less than a week, well over three in the past year and two in the past six months, at least a week apart, with no vomiting between episodes, and onset more than three months ago. The prodrome, the triggers, and relief with sleep in a dark room are typical. Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome is excluded by his history. With episodes every one to three weeks that stop his work, it is moderate to severe. The diagnosis is clinical, with no confirmatory test, so it is recorded as provisional and should be revisited if the pattern changes

Complete. The blood and urine tests, CT enterography, and upper endoscopy exclude obstruction, malrotation, mucosal disease, pancreatitis, celiac disease, and thyroid, adrenal, and metabolic causes. A gastric emptying study is not needed, as he has no symptoms of gastroparesis between episodes, and brain imaging is not needed without headache or neurological signs. Repeat testing is not advised unless an episode is atypical

A tricyclic is first line for moderate-to-severe disease. Amitriptyline at about 1 to 1.5 mg/kg is the usual effective dose, which for him is 75 to 100 mg at bedtime. His baseline QTc of 412 ms allows it. Coenzyme Q10 and riboflavin are conditional options that can be added later if the response is partial; topiramate or aprepitant are alternatives if amitriptyline fails or is not tolerated

Nasal sumatriptan with an ondansetron dissolving tablet, taken together within the first 30 to 45 minutes of the prodrome, works best. He has no heart disease, uncontrolled hypertension, or stroke that would rule out a triptan. The serotonin syndrome risk with amitriptyline is low at these doses, and he was told its warning signs

Mild anxiety (GAD-7 8) centered on episodes, without low mood. Anxiety and stress both trigger episodes and follow from them, so relaxation training and cognitive behavioral therapy are worthwhile alongside medicine. No anxiety disorder is diagnosed

recommendations: Amitriptyline 25 mg at bedtime, raised by 25 mg every two weeks to 75 mg; ECG at about 50 mg and at 75 mg, keeping the QTc below 450 ms; judge the response after three months at the target dose and continue for at least a year if it helps
Sumatriptan 20 mg nasal spray with ondansetron 8 mg dissolving tablet at the first sign of the prodrome; the spray may be repeated once after 2 hours, no more than 6 sprays a week

Emergency department letter: intravenous fluids with dextrose, intravenous ondansetron, lorazepam 1 to 2 mg if needed, a dark quiet room, a check of electrolytes and lipase, and opioids used sparingly
Trigger plan: regular small meals, regular sleep, planning around travel and social events, and early treatment of infections; continue to avoid cannabis
Relaxation breathing now, and cognitive behavioral therapy if he is willing
Keep the symptom diary and bring it to each visit
No further tests now; no gastric emptying study or brain imaging
Primary care review at about three months and six months; gastroenterology review if there is no response after three months at the target dose, or if the pattern changes
